doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

chapter: Mary Lou Williams and learning by ear
title: Playing for singers and why he took any gig
summary: He likes singers because of his wives and the Ink Spots, and recalls his father disliking bebop. He quit for a year, took a day job, and then resolved to play with anybody. He has never had a non-music job in New York.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Oh boy. That’s great. Good story. Is there a difference in playing behind singers than playing behind —

Absolutely. Absolutely. Like I said, my first wife was a singer. So I came in contact with all that that entails. And so I got to see, naturally I knew how musician, a lot of musicians hate singers, oh my goodness, “Oh here comes one,” say ohhh. But because I was married to singers and I liked singers, and my father and my aunt they played singers, I enjoyed singers. I didn’t have a problem with them. That’s how I learned, listened to the Ink Spots. That’s how I learned bass lines as a little kid. All the standards that Bill Kenny used to sing. So what’s wrong with singers. My father remembered — my father hated bebop by the way. “That’s skeet-skeet music. They don’t play the melody. Play the melody, son.”

Skeet skeet. Play the melody. “Remember that son.” Because he would ask people advising musicians, told them it’s important to learn the melody. So I didn’t have a problem with singers. And my wife would come home crying about all the dirty tricks that musicians would play on her. And so what happened with me, I played with anybody. That’s a whole ‘nother story. Before I got to New York I quit for a year and then I didn’t play for a whole year. Because I didn’t want to play rhythm & blues. I was an elitist. I only played jazz. If I couldn’t get a jazz-playing gig, if I couldn’t get a gig playing jazz no don’t call me, I don’t want that. I’m a jazz musician. But then so I went and got a day gig for a whole year. And I was miserable. So at the end of that year I started saying you know what? If I can get a job playing anything I’d do it. It’ll get me out of this damn gig. So when I came to New York that was all part of my mindset. I’ll play with anybody. That’s the other part of playing in any key, all of that. So there’s a number of factors that helped me to be able to play music. I’ve never done, since I’ve been in New York I’ve never had a job doing anything else.
Never had a day gig since you moved here?
Not non-musical. I mean there was a time I tried to find out about business but I wouldn’t make my living off of that. That was just experimenting.
Well a good musician doesn’t have to like the music they play on every gig.
You mean they just are very professional.
They just need to be professional, right?

But there again you’ve got to talk to each person. That’s philosophical. It depends where they’re coming from and then what their sentiments are and how they define themselves. You know? You have just as many musicians as you have varieties of flowers. Because we’re people and we’re different. And it’s okay. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
